questions.prompt: A team's GPU compute grows ~10x every 3 years while usable public-text corpora grow far slower. Which regime does this trajectory produce for GPT-3-scale runs?

options.label: Compute-starved — models shrink to fit the data
Data-starved — runs re-read the same unique tokens many times
Balanced — Chinchilla's ratio holds automatically at larger scale
Label-bound — the binding constraint becomes annotation, not tokens

questions.explanation: Demand outgrows unique supply, so the schedule repeats the corpus — GPT-2 re-read WebText ~17 times; GPT-3 sat at ~1.7 unique tokens per parameter. Below the fitted ~20 tok/param, extra passes buy little new signal.

questions.prompt: True or false: doubling the raw, deduplicated web corpus always doubles the total information a run learns from it.
questions.explanation: Marginal ICR decays as ~1/(O·D): the next FLOP's yield halves with each doubling. Most marginal tokens are near-duplicates of signal the model already holds.

questions.prompt: Under the chapter's illustrative model with I(D) ∝ ln D and linear per-sample compute, marginal ICR scales as:

options.label: ∝ D — it rises with more data
constant — corpus size does not change the ratio

questions.explanation: I(D) ∝ ln D gives dI/dD ∝ 1/D; with compute linear in samples, marginal ICR ∝ 1/(O_sample · D). Each doubling halves the next FLOP's learning yield — the frontier bends down.

questions.prompt: A team reduces 1,000,000 images to 100,000. Full-data training takes 10 hours; scoring costs 1 hour; subset training costs 3 hours. Does the selection inequality pass, and by what margin?
questions.explanation: T_select + T_train(sub) = 1 + 3 = 4 h < T_train(full) = 10 h, a 6-hour margin. The retained fraction (10%) is not the test — time at matched quality is.

questions.prompt: Why is MinHash + LSH preferred over exhaustive pairwise Jaccard for near-duplicate detection at corpus scale?

options.label: Pairwise comparison is quadratic in document count; sketches make detection near-linear with signatures held in RAM
It works only on text, so it is more specialized

questions.explanation: Pairwise Jaccard on ~8M documents is ~3×10^13 comparisons — infeasible. MinHash compresses each doc to a ~128-hash signature (~4.1 GB in RAM for the chapter's corpus) and LSH buckets likely near-dupes so they collide without all-pairs scans.

questions.prompt: In foundation-model amortization with pretraining at 10,000 GPU-hours, fine-tuning at 50 GPU-hours/task, and scratch training at 1,000 GPU-hours/task, the compute-only break-even is:
questions.explanation: 10,000 + 50N < 1,000N ⇒ N > 10.53 ⇒ at least 11 tasks. At N = 10 the prepaid path costs 10,500 GPU-hours against scratch's 10,000 — still behind.

questions.prompt: The selection inequality is a time inequality. Explain to a colleague why 'we pruned 40% of the dataset' is not, by itself, evidence the pipeline saved anything — name at least three terms that can quietly eat the margin.
questions.rubric: Score + subset-train < full-train at matched quality is the claim. Retained fraction alone ignores: scorer cost (can exceed the margin), coverage/quality loss on rare slices, the data-path tax (scattered 4 KB reads lose ~375x/14x/<2x bandwidth by tier), and refresh cadence (every re-score re-spends the overhead).

questions.prompt: Your ImageNet coreset hits top-1 target on 30% of the data, but the rare-class slice dropped 9 points. Using the coverage-floor framing, explain why 'the scores said these were the best examples' is not a defense.
questions.rubric: The ranking optimizes an aggregate; floors are the constraint layer enforcing per-slice representation. A rare-class regression means the subset failed its constraint — raise the floor or the budget rather than debate scores. If summed floors exceed the budget, the plan is infeasible regardless of ranking.

questions.prompt: A corpus has 20B unique tokens; the model has 2.5B parameters. (a) What is the tokens-per-parameter ratio, and is the run above or below the fitted ~20? (b) If the schedule demands 75B tokens, how many passes over the corpus does that imply?
questions.answer: (a) 20B/2.5B = 8 tok/param — below the fitted ~20, so data-starved. (b) 75B/20B = 3.75 passes — the run re-reads the corpus nearly four times.

questions.prompt: Scoring an ImageNet-scale pool costs at most one forward pass per image — about one-third of an epoch's compute. Training takes 100 epochs on full data and 100 epochs on a 10% subset (≈10x cheaper per epoch). Compute both sides of the selection inequality. What scorer cost (in epoch-equivalents) still leaves selection profitable?
questions.answer: Full side: 100 epochs. Selected side: ≤1/3 epoch + 10 epochs ≈ 10.33 epochs — clears by ~89.7. Ceiling: T_select < 100 − 10 = 90 epochs of compute; scoring could cost almost the whole run and still win. In practice quality and coverage bind first.

questions.prompt: Labels cost \$5 each; pool scoring costs \$50/round and runs 10 rounds. Compare total spend: (a) random — label 100,000; (b) active — label 50,000 to reach the same accuracy. What must hold for active learning to stay ahead as the pool grows?
questions.answer: Random: 100,000 × \$5 = \$500,000. Active: 50,000 × \$5 + 10 × \$50 = \$250,500 — about \$249,500 saved. The advantage survives only if per-round scoring stays sub-linear in pool size; an all-pool rescore every round reintroduces the cost the loop was meant to avoid.
